'''''Protea magnifica''''', commonly known as the '''queen protea''',<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=Wiersema1999>{{cite book |title= World Economic Plants: A Standard Reference |first= John H. |last=Wiersema| first2= Blanca | last2= León |edition= illustrated |publisher= CRC Press |year= 1999 |isbn= 978-0-8493-2119-1 |page= 693}}</ref><ref name=BioEx>{{cite web |title=''Protea magnifica'' (Queen protea) |url=http://biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/proteaceae/protea_magnifica.htm |website=Biodiversity Explorer |publisher=Iziko - Museums of South Africa |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref> is a [[shrub]],<ref name=ProAtlWeb>{{cite web |title=Bearded Sugarbushes - ''Proteas'' |url=https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/sugar2.htm |date=11 March 1998 |website=Protea Atlas Project Website |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref> which belongs to the genus ''[[Protea]]'' within the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Proteaceae]],<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=BioEx/> and which is native to [[South Africa]].<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=PoWO/>

The species is also called '''queen sugarbush''',<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=ProAtlWeb/> '''bearded sugarbush''' or '''woolly beard'''. In the [[Afrikaans language]] the [[vernacular name]]s {{lang|af|baardprotea}}, {{lang|af|baardsuikerbos}}, {{lang|af|baard-suikerbos}}, {{lang|af|koninginprotea}}, {{lang|af|suikerbosprotea}}, {{lang|af|wolbaardsuikerbos}} and {{lang|af|wolbaard-suikerbos}} have all been recorded for the plant.<ref name=SANBI/>

==Taxonomy==
The [[International Plant Names Index]] attributes the authorship of ''Protea magnifica'' to [[Henry Cranke Andrews]],<ref name=IPNI>{{Cite web |title=''Protea magnifica'' |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/705936-1 |website=[[International Plant Names Index]] |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref> but the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] attributes it to [[Johann Heinrich Friedrich Link]].<ref name=SANBI/>

==Description==
It grows either as an erect or as a sprawling [[shrub]], growing up to {{Convert|2.5|m|ft}} in height. The inflorescences are specialised structures called [[Pseudanthium|pseudanthia]], also known simply as [[flower head]]s, containing hundred of reduced flowers, called [[floret]]s. It is [[monoecious]], both sexes occur in each flower.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> It blooms in spring,<ref name=BioEx/> from June to January. The fruit, containing a seed, is kept within the old, dried [[infructescence]] which is retained persistently on the plant.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

==Distribution==
This plant is [[endemic]] to the Cape Region of South Africa,<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=PoWO/> where it only occurs in the [[Western Cape]] province.<ref name=SANBI/> It occurs in the [[Koue Bokkeveld]] to [[Hottentots Holland]], [[Klein Swartberg]], [[Riviersonderend Mountains|Riviersonderend]],<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> [[Stellenbosch#Climate and geography|Franschhoek]]<ref name=BioEx/> and central [[Langeberg]] mountain ranges. It is spatially distributed as isolated stands.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

==Ecology==
It is [[Pollination|pollinated]] by birds. The [[wildfire]]s which periodically move through the land in which the shrub grows destroy the adult plants, but the seeds can survive such an event. When released, the seeds are dispersed by means of the wind.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

===Habitat===
It grows high in the mountains on hot, dry mountain slopes near the snow line, at altitudes between {{Convert|1,200 and 2,700|m}}.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> It exclusively occurs in a [[fynbos]] [[habitat]], but it occur in many different sub-types of this general habitat. It usually grows in substrates derived of [[sandstone]], but may sometimes grow on [[quartzite]].<ref name=SANBI/>

==Uses==
This the most prized [[cut flower]] in the trade. In 1998, the best flower heads were still said come from the wild, and were often harvested for this purpose.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

==Conservation==
''Protea magnifica'' is not threatened,<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=ProAtlWeb/> and is locally common.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> As of 2019 the total population numbers were believed to be stable. The [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] first assessed this species for the [[Regional Red List|Red List of South African Plants]] in 2009, rating the conservation status as ''[[least concern]]''. In 2019 this assessment was reiterated.<ref name=SANBI/>
